title: モスクワでテロ計画 米が露に警告
body: ［モスクワ　３１日　ロイター］ - ロシア連邦保安局（ＦＳＢ）は、モス‌クワでのテロ攻撃の準⁠備に関する情報を、米国からパートナー間の既存ルー​トを通じて受け取ったと明らかにした。適切‌な措置を取っているという。モスクワの米大使館はこ‌れとは別に、‌モスクワ南部のツァリ​ツィノ博物館保護区で「大量の‌死傷者が出る事態の確かな脅威を把握し‌ている」​とし、米政府がロシア当局‌と連携していると表明した。ロシア⁠のＲＩＡ通信はロシアの法執行機関の話として、ツァリツィノ博物館保⁠護区が一時閉鎖され、​公園への‌立ち入りが現在制限されていると報じた。同保護区は宮殿⁠博物館と公園が一体になっ⁠た施設。米大使館は２０２４年３月初め、過激派⁠がモスクワで攻撃を計画していると警告。３月２２日‌にモ⁠スクワ郊外のコンサート会​場を武装集団が襲撃し、１４０人以上が死亡した。

title: GMO攻撃者 被害者サイト開設か
body:
GMOインターネットグループへの不正アクセス問題で、被害者同士の情報共有をうたって立ち上げられたサイトと、犯行声明を載せていたサイトに、設計図に当たる「ソースコード」の構成など多くの共通点があることが31日、分かった。情報共有サイトは、GMOが被害を公表した10月21日より前に開設が準備されていたことも判明。攻撃側が被害者を集めGMOに圧力をかけ、交渉を有利に進めようとした疑いがある。共同通信がセキュリティー専門家の協力を得て分析した。【写真】119万円の損失が出た取引画面　GMO利用者、不正アクセスで
サイト名は「情報共有フォーラム」。ほとんど閲覧されておらず、既に閉鎖されている。サイトの痕跡を調べると、ソースコードが、犯行声明のサイトと一部同じだったことに加え、全体の構成も酷似していた。さらに同じ米国のレンタルサーバー事業者を使っていた。コードには日本語も使われていた。画像や文章を保管していたフォルダー名も一致。閲覧者が、サイト内で、どのフォルダーを見られるかという権限の決め方も一緒だった。

title: 米大統領 造反・不祥事議員を称賛
body: 【ワシントン＝杉本康士】トランプ米大統領は10月31日、米中間選挙の投開票日が11月3日に迫る中で複数の州の選挙集会に電話を通じて参加し、与党・共和党候補への投票を呼び掛けた。共和党に厳しい情勢が伝えられており、トランプ氏はこれまで距離を置いてきた候補を支持する考えも表明。1議席でも多く獲得するため、なりふり構わない姿を見せている。【写真】妻メラニアさんにキスしようとするも、帽子のつばに阻まれるトランプ氏トランプ氏は10月31日午前に南部フロリダ州のゴルフ場で過ごし、午後には私邸マールアラーゴに戻って中西部のオハイオ州やミシガン州などで開かれた集会に電話で参加を告知。トランプ氏の政治団体は30日、投開票までに少なくとも19州の選挙集会に参加する予定だと発表していた。共和党の苦戦が予想される中、トランプ氏は自身に批判的な議員や、不祥事を理由にトランプ氏自身が出馬断念を促していた議員への投票を呼び掛けた。下院フロリダ州27区で出馬しているサラザール下院議員はトランプ政権の強引な不法移民取り締まりを批判。トランプ氏は同選挙区の候補変更を求める動きに同調していたが、31日にはSNSで「住民を代表する素晴らしい仕事をしている！」と称賛した。また、下院オハイオ州7区のミラー下院議員は元妻と子供への暴力が報じられ、トランプ氏は出馬を取りやめるよう伝えたとされる。だが、31日に「ミラーはオハイオ州7区の素晴らしい住民にとって最高の擁護者だ！」とSNSに投稿し、支持を訴えた。選挙戦は最終盤に入り、政治分析サイト「クック・ポリティカル・リポート」は30日に下院選12選挙区の評価を変更。いずれも当初予測よりも民主党候補が善戦していると指摘した。過半数218のところ、最大240議席を獲得すると予測している。上院の過半数争いは不透明としつつ、「民主党がわずかに有利」とした。

title: 学校で突然言葉出ず 悩んだ吃音
body:
■「誰かの力になりたい」思いを伝える女子大学生思うように言葉が出てこない。そんな「吃音」の症状と向き合いながら、演劇や啓発活動で思いを伝える女子大学生がいます。【写真を見る】ご当地ヒーロー「桜花爛漫ミマラブリー」を演じる安岡さん吃音は、言葉に詰まったり同じ言葉を繰り返したりする、発話障害の一つで、全国で約100人に1人の割合で、約120万人に症状があるとされています。女子大学生は吃音で悩んだ過去があるからこそ、今度は誰かの力になりたいと話します。■ご当地ヒーローとして活躍「そこまでよ、悪党ども。食と子どもと福祉を守る一輪の花、桜花爛漫ミマラブリー!」美作大学のマスコットキャラクターで、ご当地ヒーローとしても活躍する「ミマラブリー」。演じているのは、高知県芸西村出身で、社会福祉学科3年生の安岡未来さんです。（美作大学社会福祉学科3年　安岡未来さん）「ミマラブリーのときは、ほんとにかわいい感じのキャラで、でもちょっと知的でクールな感じだよなっていうのを意識しながら、声を当てたり動きをやっています」ともにヒーローショーを行うメンバーは、演じるときと普段とのギャップが魅力だと話します。（美作大学児童学科3年　金堂優太さん）「普段はおしとやかな感じで、静かで知的なイメージがあるんですけど、『ミマラブリー』に入っているときは生き生きとしていて、キャラにすごく合っているなと思います。芯がしっかりあって、クールな女ヒーローみたいな感じのイメージです」■中学生の時に突然言葉が出てこなくなった生き生きと舞台に立つ安岡さんですが、実は、言葉が滑らかに出てこない「吃音」の症状があります。今はほとんどなくなりましたが、それでも授業の発表などで緊張すると、言葉に詰まることがあるといいます。初めて症状が出たのは、中学1年の秋。放送委員として、いつものように校内放送をしようとした時、突然、言葉が出てこなくなったのです。（美作大学社会福祉学科3年　安岡未来さん）「それまでは普通に喋れていたし、友だちと会話もできていたので、給食の放送の出来事がきっかけで、どんどん話せなくなっていったという感じです。みんなに、この話し方のことを思われたらどうしようみたいな」当時、中学生だった安岡さんは悪化していく症状に不安を覚えるとともに、周囲から向けられる視線やひやかし、そして自分の気持ちをうまく表現できないもどかしさに苦しむことになります。
【後編】へ続く舞台を通して「吃音」への理解を広めたい…悩んだ過去と向き合い前へ進む女子大学生「過去の自分のように、助けを必要とする子どもたちを救える立場になりたい」

title: ハロウィン 渋谷に集まった人の声
body:
今年もハロウィーンがやってきた。2026年10月31日は土曜日。ハロウィーン当日が土曜日と重なるのは、コロナ禍のさなかだった2020年以来、6年ぶりだ。渋谷区は「GOODBYE BAD HALLOWEEN」を合言葉に、今年も厳戒態勢を敷いた。【実際の画像】「区長、来てごめんね」ナンパ男、おばけ、顔面ピアスだらけのコスプレ姿…6年ぶりの土曜開催《2026年渋谷ハロウィーン》の様子を写真で一気に見る仮装した若者が路上に集い、見知らぬ者同士で写真を撮り合う。渋谷は、日本におけるハロウィーンの楽しみ方のひとつを築いた街でもある。規制の網が幾重にもかかるなか、今年の渋谷はどんなハロウィーンの夜を迎えたのか。◆◆◆
日本でハロウィーンが催しとして姿を見せたのは1983年、原宿のキデイランドが販売促進の一環として、表参道で仮装パレードを開いたのが最初だという。1997年には東京ディズニーランドがハロウィーンのプログラムを始め、同じ年に川崎駅前で「カワサキハロウィン」のパレードもスタートした。テーマパークと商店街が、子どもの行事だったハロウィーンを、大人が仮装して楽しむ日に変えていった。そうした流れが、主催者のいない“路上の祭り”として花開いたのが渋谷のハロウィーンだ。2010年代に入ると、ハチ公前やセンター街に仮装した若者が自然発生的に集まるようになった。見知らぬ者同士が写真を撮り合う光景はテレビやSNSで広まり、海外からも注目を集めた。
だが熱狂は、路上飲酒やごみ、痴漢や暴行といったトラブルも連れてきた。象徴的だったのが2018年、センター街で群衆が軽トラックを横転させた事件だ。渋谷区は翌2019年に条例を定め、ハロウィーン時期の駅周辺での夜間の路上飲酒を禁じた。2022年に韓国・梨泰院で雑踏事故が起きると、区の姿勢はさらに硬くなる。2023年、長谷部健区長は「渋谷はハロウィーンイベントの会場ではありません」と世界に向けて発信し、ハチ公前を封鎖。この年のピーク時の来街者は、予想の6万人に対して1万5000人にとどまった。2024年10月からは、渋谷駅周辺での18時から翌朝5時までの路上飲酒が、ハロウィーン期間に限らず通年で禁止されている。規制が強まるにつれ、ハロウィーンの人波は渋谷の外へと広がり、各区が対応を迫られている。池袋では、豊島区と企業が組む「池袋ハロウィンコスプレフェス」が今年も30日から3日間の日程で開かれている。約400人のコスプレイヤーが大通りを練り歩くパレードも組まれ、昨年は3日間で16万1000人が訪れた。主催者がいて、参加ルールもある“管理されたハロウィーン”だ。新宿区も歌舞伎町周辺でハロウィーン期間中の路上飲酒を規制し、警戒を強めた。

title: 日米豪印外相会談 AIなど協力確認
body: 日本とアメリカ、オーストラリア、インドによる「クアッド」の外相会談がアメリカで行われ、AI=人工知能技術への対応などで協力していくことを確認しました。【写真で見る】日米豪印4か国「クアッド」外相会談　茂木外務大臣ら外相らの写真撮影「クアッド」外相会談はG20にあわせて31日、アメリカで行われ、日本からは茂木外務大臣が出席しました。発表された成果文書によりますと、4か国は中国を念頭に、恣意的な輸出規制や経済的威圧に深刻な懸念を表明しました。また、ホルムズ海峡などにおける航行の自由の必要性をあらためて強調しました。AIについては、経済成長に重要であることを強調する一方、混乱が生じる前に、脆弱性などを特定する新たな取り組みを始めるとしています。その上でインド太平洋地域全域で信頼できるAIへのアクセスを支援するため、およそ8500万ドル=日本円で130億円を超える財政支援を行う意向を表明しました。このほか、オンライン詐欺について深刻な懸念を表明し、犯罪組織の責任を追及する方針を確認しました。

title: ウが製油所攻撃再開 ロシア副首相
body: 【AFP＝時事】ロシアのアレクサンドル・ノバク副首相は30日、ウクライナが一時中断していた製油所への攻撃を再開したと述べ、ロシアが計画する軽油（ディーゼル燃料）の輸出量が減少する可能性があると警告した。ウクライナ側からのコメントは今のところない。【関連記事】トランプ氏の対ロ制裁停止、世界経済への影響分析のため ルビオ米国務長官ドナルド・トランプ米大統領は数週間にわたり、ウクライナによる攻撃が軽油価格上昇の原因だとして、攻撃を中止するよう同国に圧力をかけてきた。一方、専門家は燃料価格の上昇を、米国とイスラエルが2月に開始した対イラン戦争と関連付けている。エネルギー問題を担当するノバク氏は国営テレビの記者に対し、「夜間にロシアの石油精製施設への攻撃があった。具体的には製油所3か所とガス化学コンビナート1か所だ」と述べた。さらに「一定期間、攻撃は途絶えていたが、きょう製油所への攻撃が再開された」と付け加えた。ロシアの通信アプリ「テレグラム」の複数のチャンネルには、ウクライナ国境から800キロ離れたロシア・サマラ州の製油所が夜間にドローン攻撃を受け、煙が立ち上る様子を捉えたとされる動画が投稿された。同州知事はテレグラムで、ウクライナのドローン攻撃により男性2人が死亡したと発表した。トランプ氏は10月初め、ロシアのウラジーミル・プーチン大統領と、ロシアが世界市場に軽油を供給するのと引き換えに対ロ制裁を緩和することで合意したが、これがウクライナと同国を支援する欧州諸国の強い反発を招いた。ノバク氏は30日、この合意に基づき、ロシアが10月に約51万トンの軽油を世界市場に出荷したと説明。「11月はさらに多くの量を計画している」と述べ、約215万トンを見込んでいるとした。ただ、ウクライナによる製油所への攻撃で、「わずかかもしれないが、供給量が減少する可能性は確かにある」と警告し、「ウクライナのドローンによるわが国の製油所への攻撃は、世界市場にとって明らかに有害だ」と非難した。【翻訳編集】 AFPBB News

title: 中間選挙 アメリカ政治にどう影響
body: 11月3日に投開票が行われるアメリカの中間選挙。この選挙では何が決まり、今後のアメリカ政治や国際社会にどのような影響があるのでしょうか。【写真で見る】物価高に苦しむ有権者の選択は？トランプ氏もオバマ氏も激戦州ミシガン入り中間選挙は、4年に1度行われるアメリカ大統領選挙の間に行われることから名付けられました。選挙では、連邦議会の上下両院議員や州知事らが選ばれます。大統領は対象になりませんが、政権への評価が投票行動に影響を与えることが多いことから、大統領の「中間テスト」とも位置づけられていて、大統領選挙と並ぶ大型選挙です。中間選挙に対する関心が高い理由は、大統領の政権運営に大きな影響を与えるためです。現在の連邦議会は、上院、下院ともに与党共和党が過半数を占めていて、トランプ大統領にとって政策や人事を進めやすい状況です。中間選挙で共和党が勝利した場合はこうした状況が維持されますが、上院と下院のいずれかで野党民主党が過半数を奪い返した場合には、トランプ氏が望む予算や法案が成立しにくくなります。さらに、議会によるトランプ氏への調査や弾劾訴追が行われる可能性も指摘されています。中間選挙では与党が議席を減らすケースが多く、第1次トランプ政権時代の2018年の選挙では、下院で過半数割れとなったことから弾劾訴追が行われ、政権への打撃となりました。こうしたことから、連邦議会議員の選挙結果が最も注目されているのです。中間選挙では、州全体が選挙区の上院は定数100のうちの3分の1が改選。今回は補欠選挙を含めた35議席が争われ、下院は435議席全てが対象です。現在の情勢について、選挙分析機関「クック・ポリティカル・リポート」は、上院が接戦で、下院は民主党が過半数を奪還する可能性が高まっていると分析しています。具体的には、上院は共和党が19議席を得られれば多数派を維持し、民主党は現有から4議席を増やせれば逆転となります。テキサス州やミシガン州など7州が接戦で、両党が激しい選挙戦を展開しています。一方、下院は民主党の優勢議席が222となっていて、過半数の218議席を上回る可能性が出ています。トランプ氏が行ったイラン攻撃の影響によるガソリン価格高騰などが逆風になっているかたちです。共和党が上下両院で過半数を確保した場合には、「トランプ政治」が継続されることになりますが、一方でも落とした場合には求心力の低下は避けられません。選挙後、内政が停滞した場合には、トランプ氏が外交に突破口を見出し、成果のための妥協に踏み切るのではないかとの懸念も出ています。中間選挙の結果は日本をはじめとする国際社会にも大きな影響を与えるため、世界がその行方に注目しています。

title: 米国版凱旋門 建設中止求め提訴
body: 【ワシントン共同】米首都ワシントンと、隣接する南部バージニア州は10月31日、トランプ政権が計画するワシントン市内での凱旋門の建設差し止めを求めて連邦地裁に提訴した。凱旋門の高さが法令で定められた建築物の高さの上限を超える上、建設に必要な議会の承認も得ていないなどとして違法だと主張した。トランプ大統領は今年が米建国250年に当たることに合わせて建設計画を主導。ワシントン中心部の観光名所リンカーン記念堂からアーリントン記念橋を渡ったポトマック川の対岸に建設を予定する。凱旋門の頂上には翼がある黄金色の自由の女神像を据える。訴状によると、凱旋門の高さは約76メートルで、市内の連邦議会議事堂やワシントン記念塔といった象徴的な建物の景観上の存在感を守るために設けられた高さの制限約40メートルを大幅に超える。政府側は必要な承認が得られれば11月5日にも建設を始める方針を示しており、司法審査が終わる前に既成事実化しようとしていると指摘した。

title: 政府 デフレ脱却宣言は慎重に判断
body: 日銀が基調的な物価上昇率が目標の2％に届いたと表明したことに対し、政府は「デフレ脱却」を宣言するかについて引き続き慎重に判断する構えだ。【ひと目でわかる】物価安定目標2％到達までの主な出来事野党からは「政府はいち早く宣言すべきだ」（国民民主党の玉木雄一郎代表）と、インフレ対策を重視する姿勢をより明確にするよう求める声が上がった。木原稔官房長官は30日の記者会見で、デフレ脱却宣言を出すかについて問われ、「物価が持続的に下落する状況を脱するだけでなく、再びそうした状況に戻る見込みがないと判断できる経済状況が必要だ」と従来の見解を改めて表明。「慎重に判断する必要があるとの考えに変わりはない」と語った。高市早苗首相は7月の記者会見で「デフレを脱却したと言える状況にない」と説明していた。そもそも首相官邸内には「宣言にはあまり意味がない」（首相周辺）との意見もあり、中東情勢などに起因する物価高への対策に重点を置いている。政府関係者は「首相の掲げる『責任ある積極財政』は需要ではなく、供給力を上げる。むしろインフレを抑制する」と解説した。ただ、第2次安倍政権以降の歴代政権がデフレ脱却を目指してきたことが、高市政権が金融緩和と積極財政を維持する背景にあるとの見方は根強い。第2次安倍政権と日銀は2013年に2％の物価上昇率を目指す共同声明を公表した。見直しについて、木原氏は「策定時点とは経済、物価の状況に大きな変化があった」と述べたものの、明言は避けた。一方、玉木氏は30日の党代議士会で「物価高騰対策をしながら、デフレ脱却宣言ができないのは変な話だ」と批判。公明党の西田実仁幹事長は会見で「いよいよインフレの時代だ。税制を含めてしっかり見直す必要がある」と訴えた。民主改革の会の小川淳也代表は「（生産コスト上昇による）コストプッシュ型、円安要因のインフレを望んでいたのか」と疑問を呈した。

title: GMOが11/2に記者会見 社長出席
body:
GMOインターネットグループが不正アクセス問題に関する記者会見を11月2日に開く方針であることが31日、分かった。熊谷正寿社長が出席し、一連の経緯や現段階で判明した事実関係を説明する見通し。GMOが記者会見するのは、問題発生以降初めて。【表】GMO不正アクセスの経過　攻撃者、被害サイト開設か　GMO公表前に開設準備
熊谷氏はこれまで、インターネット上で会社の対応方針を発信していた。25日付のブログで、警察や自衛隊が攻撃元のサーバーに入り込んで被害を防ぐ「能動的サイバー防御」の適用を国に要請した意図を説明。29日には交流サイト（SNS）に「犯人の特定につながる有力な情報を警察に提出予定」と書き込んでいた。

title: GMO 24年にシステム脆弱性指摘
body:
ＧＭＯインターネットのクラウドサービスが不正アクセスを受け、利用者とみられる個人情報が公開された問題で、グループのセキュリティー会社が２０２４年にシステムの脆弱（ぜいじゃく）性を指摘していたことがわかった。親会社のＧＭＯインターネットグループの熊谷正寿会長兼社長は１１月２日にも記者会見を開き、一連の経緯を説明する見通しだ。【一覧表】個人情報流出が判明した企業・団体と問い合わせ先
関係者によると、指摘したのはグループ企業の「ＧＭＯサイバーセキュリティｂｙイエラエ」。同社は「ホワイトハッカー」と呼ばれるサイバー分野の専門家を多数抱えている。
熊谷氏は、自身の１０月２５日のブログで、システムの問題点の指摘を社内から受けていたが、サービスへの影響などを考慮した結果、対応が遅れたと明らかにしていた。

title: 出国時に返金 新免税制度が開始
body: 訪日外国人客（インバウンド）を対象にした消費税の新たな免税制度が11月1日から始まった。店頭で消費税込みの価格で販売し、出国時に消費税分を返金する「リファンド（返金）方式」に変更する。免税品の不正転売対策が目的。現行の免税制度が1952年に導入されてから約74年ぶりの抜本改革となる。【写真で見る】11月１日スタートの新しい免税制度10月末までの旧方式では、旅行客が街中の免税店で5000円以上の商品を買った際、パスポートを提示すれば消費税抜きの価格で購入でき、出国時に税関が確認する方式を取っていた。ただ、免税品を国外に持ち出さずに日本国内で転売して、消費税分の利ざやを稼ぐ行為が相次いでいた。新方式では、免税店で旅行客が税込み価格で購入する。出国時に免税店で提示したパスポートを専用端末や専用ウェブサイトで照合。必要に応じて税関が免税品を所持しているか確認する。その後、クレジットカードや現金などで消費税分が返金されるが、免税品が確認できないと返金されない。新方式では、衣類や家電などの一般物品と食品などの消耗品の区分をやめ、消耗品に設けている1日1店舗当たり50万円の購入上限額も撤廃する。免税品を指定袋で特殊包装する必要もなくなる。【妹尾直道】

title: ブラックフライデー 先行セールも
body:
米国発祥の大型商戦「ブラックフライデー」が早くも熱を帯びている。11月下旬の本格化に先駆け、一部の流通大手は10月末からフライングセールを開始した。物価高で消費者の財布のひもが固くなる中、各社はクーポンや限定品を用意し、家電や生活雑貨で例年より一足先に「お得感」を競う。セール期間を延ばし、受注や配送の混雑を分散させる狙いもある。【画像】ビール、値下げで商戦熱気　主力商品刷新、販売を強化
ブラックフライデーは米国の感謝祭翌日の金曜日を指す。今年は11月27日に当たり、小売業界有数の大型商戦として日本でも定着している。調査会社クロス・マーケティング（東京）によると国内の認知率は昨年の調査で計85.8％に達した。イオンは、昨年より前倒しして10月31日から「イオンスタイルオンライン」で先行セールを実施。取り扱うほぼ全商品に使える15％オフクーポンを用意した。ディスカウント店「ドン・キホーテ」の運営会社も10月末から先行販売を始めた。「アピタ・ピアゴ　オンラインショップ」は高額酒やブランド時計を会員限定で販売。ドンキも家電や車用品など100商品以上を割引価格で店頭に並べた。

title: 'We came back from hell', say Ukrainians after years in Russia-occupied front-line city
summary: One evacuated couple says they crossed minefields in Oleshky in search of food.
body:
Emotional reunions with loved ones for Oleshky evacuees
Warning: This story contains graphic content.
Olha has one word to describe what life has been like in the front-line city of Oleshky over the past few years: "Horror".
Disembarking alongside her from a coach in the Ukrainian region of Chernihiv with their immediate family and dog, her husband Viacheslav put it this way: "We came back from hell."
The couple were among hundreds of residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city who crossed into northern Ukraine via Belarus on Saturday, many reuniting with loved ones they had not seen for years.
Oleshky, seized by Russia during the first few days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022, is trapped on one side by the Dnipro River and on the other side by Russian forces.
Olha and Viacheslav had lived there with their son and daughter, both in their 30s. Even as the shelling around them intensified, they feared that trying to escape could be even more dangerous, with routes mined and subject to drone attack.
As supplies dwindled, the couple said they made an attempt to find food by crossing through minefields earlier this month. "People were stepping on mines, dying and being maimed, all just to survive," Olha told the BBC.
Those who were too afraid to go out in the city had resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive.
"We saw that the situation wasn't getting any better, so we realised we had to get out," Olha said.
Viacheslav and his wife Olha were living in Oleshky with their children
That opportunity came earlier this week when a humanitarian ceasefire, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, took effect in the Kherson region, providing the first few days of peace in the area for four years and allowing Oleshky residents to evacuate.
Up to 6,000 people, including 200 children, were believed to still be living in Oleshky and its surrounding areas, with 1,700 in the city itself.
Residents had a four-hour window on Friday to leave, with a convoy of 25 buses brought in for up to 750 evacuees, along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.
After travelling through Russian-occupied territory to southern Russia, then flying to Belarus, evacuees arrived on buses to a military facility in Chernihiv on Saturday.
On the tarmac, where evacuees were processed before travelling onwards, some elderly residents were so weak they had to be carried on stretchers.
For many, there were emotional reunions.
Mykhailo Palii says the situation in the city "kept getting worse and worse"
As Mykhailo Palii arrived, his daughters Dasha and Anya, who thought they might never see him again, sprinted across the tarmac screaming and crying.
After an emotional embrace, Palii described a glimpse of life in Oleshky, although he said he had, until then, kept many of the details from his family.
"A hole was blown into the bathroom," he said. "There were drone attacks and missile strikes. It happened, but I didn't tell them about it because I knew they would worry."
Volodymyr (L) and Tetiana (R) say they feared the journey out of Oleshky could have been disrupted
Tetiana and Volodymyr, a couple carrying a cat when they arrived in Chernihiv, said their entire home was burned down three years ago, and they had been living in the abandoned house of a neighbour since.
For them, leaving as soon as it was safe to do so was an easy decision. "There's nothing for us to regret leaving. We don't have relatives there. Our children are married and don't live with us in the city," said Tetiana.
But those who managed to escape also worry about those left behind. "There are still a lot of people left there, living under those conditions," said Olha.
Now that the evacuees have left Oleshky, they will also face a new challenge - working out where to go next and how to rebuild their lives.
Palii said he would look for a job so he can provide for his family: "There's no job I can't handle. Digging, hoeing, planting, building. I can even do demolition work."
Olha said she and her family have no relatives elsewhere in Ukraine, and they will stay with some acquaintances for an extended period while they get back on their feet.
"If we managed to survive in hell, we'll survive here too."

title: Ukrainian evacuees reunite with family after years trapped in Russia-occupied city
summary: Oleshky residents had been without food, water and electricity, with many resorting to cooking garden weeds to survive.
body:
Watch: Evacuees from Oleshky reunited with their families
There were raw emotional scenes as people evacuated from the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky crossed from Belarus into the Ukrainian region of Chernihiv.
Families cried as they reunited with relatives they had not seen for years, with two sisters running and crying out as they embraced their father.
Some elderly residents were so weak they were carried on stretchers. They had been trapped in the frontline city without food, water and electricity, with many resorting to cooking garden weeds to survive.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky thanked US First Lady Melania Trump for her efforts in brokering a local ceasefire that paved the way for their evacuation on Friday.
Upon their arrival, Dasha and Anya Palii sprinted across the tarmac screaming towards the bus carrying their father Mykhailo.
Their cries and their tears captured the sheer relief of three years of desperate worry, fearing they would never see him again.
Their mother Zhanna clasped Mykhailo's face and stroked his forehead again and again, as if checking he was the same man she had left behind. He promised her, finally, they will now get married.
Tetiana and Volodymyr, an older couple carrying their cat, told the BBC they no longer have a home, after it was burned down in the first year of the war. They have been living in the abandoned house of a neighbour.
They said they instantly took the decision to leave but feared their journey could be disrupted. Now they have to work out where to go next and how to rebuild their lives.
Another couple also made it out with their cat
Ukrainian military positions lie just 5km (3.1 miles) from Oleshky, but evacuees first had to travel through Russian-occupied territory to southern Russia, where they flew to Belarus, before finally being driven across Ukraine's northern border on Saturday.
The oldest evacuee was 94 years old, while the youngest was one, according to Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman.
Zelensky said in a post on X that "all of them will receive the assistance they need. It is important that government agencies and all the regional and local authorities involved work effectively and help our people adapt."
Many people bear the scars: the convoy includes as many ambulances as coaches. The impact of years caught between the frontlines is written on the weary faces of many of Oleshky's residents, some hobbling on crutches, others needing wheelchairs.
They have a lot to come to terms with, not least having left the place they call home.
A humanitarian ceasefire took effect across the frontline region of Kherson on Tuesday, providing the first few days of peace in the area in four years, following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Before the war, Oleshky was home to 24,000 people.
Conditions had become so desperate in the city that not only was getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escape was highly dangerous because the routes out had been mined and subject to drone attack.
Bridges across the nearby River Dnipro have been destroyed and sources say the riverbank has been mined and is dangerous.
One resident who fled the city three weeks earlier told the BBC he had walked through 24km (15 miles) of minefields to get to safety.
The ceasefire allowed the road out of the city to be cleared of mines and humanitarian aid to be delivered.
Ceasefire measures will remain in place until the end of Sunday 1 November.
Residents had a four-hour window to leave before a convoy of 25 buses, with space for 750 people, left the town on Friday afternoon - along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.
Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay in the war-torn city, despite widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water.
Some of the older generation did not want to leave,one relative told the BBC.
Lubinets said on Friday morning that those who decided to stay "will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance".
He and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky together on Friday, setting off from Armiansk, in the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula.
Lubinets is the first Ukrainian official since the start of the war to visit Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.
Zelensky praised him and his team for helping move evacuees out to safety.
The Ukrainian president also thanked those who had helped bring attention to the "true humanitarian catastrophe in Ukrainian territory temporarily occupied by Russia".
The ceasefire has required close cooperation between Lubinets and Lantratova, which Lubinets said he carried out in the interests of saving lives.
But some in Ukraine have recoiled at the sight of him standing beside a representative of the Russian occupying power which has killed so many of the city's residents and made life unbearable for the rest.
Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators.
Despite the ceasefire in Oleshky, the war has continued.
Zelensky said that Russia had attacked Ukrainian energy infrastructure, hitting electricity substations, thermal power plants and gas infrastructure.
Ukraine's military said it hit a major Russian producer of missile fuel in the Rostov region.
Negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US are due to resume ceasefire talks in Abu Dhabi in early November after discussions were suspended earlier this year due to the Iran war.

body:
Hundreds of thousands of protesters demonstrated across France as the country prepares for a general strike in the coming days.
In Paris, police fired tear gas and clashed with protesters in a third weekend of nationwide demonstrations against the rising cost of living and poor public services.
More than 320,000 people took to the streets around the country and at least 290 protesters were arrested, according to France's interior ministry. Police say about 70,000 demonstrated in Paris.
The authorities prepared extensively to avoid a repeat of the violence, rioting and looting that happened two weeks ago.
Protests also took place in Albania, Germany and Italy as youth take to the streets across Europe, the BBC's correspondent James Waterhouse reports.

title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
summary: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) says North Korea was responsible for the hack.
body:
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn)assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.
The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added.
Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so.
"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the hack.
Two analytics firmspreviously told the BBCthey had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.
Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.
All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said.
From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they mean
The company said its next goal is resuming withdrawal services for users, saying it remained on track to reopen withdrawals on Sunday 1 November and would provide a further update once details were confirmed.
The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible.
North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks.
Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach".
Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".
On Friday, the company said it had frozen around $3bn of stolen assets after working with law enforcement, intelligence firms and partners.
The investigation is ongoing, it added. The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.
Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.
Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.

title: India's opposition set to hold mega rally seeking election chief's resignation
summary: It comes amid growing protests over a voter roll revision exercise feared to leave 130 million voters off rolls.
body:
Rahul Gandhi has called on people to gather at the protest site in large numbers
Tens of thousands of people are expected to gather in the Indian capital, Delhi, for a mega opposition rally, seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner and electoral reforms.
The rally, called by the main opposition Congress party, will begin around noon at the famous Ramlila Maidan grounds, with leaders claiming a million people could attend.
Several top leaders of the Congress-led INDIA alliance have said they would attend and the influential Gen Z-led pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has also pledged support.
The rally comes amid growing criticism of a voter-list revision exercise that has removed 130 million names from the draft rolls across India.
The Election Commission of India (ECI) says the exercise is aimed at updating the voters' list by purging names of people who have died or moved away from their registered addresses.
But opposition parties allege that the exercise - known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) - could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) by removing eligible voters from the rolls. They accuse the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and the BJP of "vote chori (theft)". Both the BJP and the ECI have denied the allegations.
The controversy intensified in September when The Indian Express newspaper in itsinvestigation,externalreported that the CEC, Gyanesh Kumar, made key decisions related to the exercise without the agreement of the two other election commissioners, who had raised objectionson more than a dozen occasions.
Protests have been going on for weeks seeking CEC Kumar's resignation and electoral reforms
The Election Commission said differences of opinion were normal in any institution and did not affect its functioning.
But concerns over the revision process have continued, with the opposition parties, the CJP and student groups organising a number of protests in Delhi and other Indian cities.
Last month, Congress MP and leader of the opposition Rahul Gandhi led tens of thousands of protesters in a march from Connaught Place in central Delhi to the Supreme Court, seeking the CEC's resignation.
"The march was just the trailer," a party leader told the BBC, adding that "Sunday's rally will be several times bigger than that".
Ahead of the rally, Gandhi said their protest was against "the demolition of Indian democracy", adding that "all the opposition parties and everybody who wants to come, political or non-political, is welcome".
"There is huge anger, huge emotional pain because millions are being disenfranchised," he said.
"We are all standing together because we are defending the Constitution. We are defending the idea of India. We are defending the vote, which is the expression of all Indians."
Thousands gathered for the last Congress rally in Delhi on 12 October
Delhi police have given permission to hold Sunday's rally, but it comes with several conditions. Media reports say the rally must end by 5pm, CCTV cameras must be installed at the venue and no marches will be allowed outside the designated protest site.
The planned mega rally has also divided opinion among traders in Chandni Chowk, one of Delhi's oldest and busiest markets, located less than a kilometre from Ramlila Maidan.
Earlier this week, a group of traders said the protest could hurt business during the festive season, coming just a week before Diwali.
But a rival group of traders said they supported Gandhi's rally and criticised the BJP for taking out a march through the market on Thursday, saying that disrupted the festive season more.
Leaders of the ruling BJP party also carried out a march in Chandni Chowk market on Thursday
Authorities have deployed thousands of police and paramilitary personnel across the city, including the roads leading up to Ramlila Grounds, Sunday's protest venue.
The opposition, which has been preparing for the rally for days now, has accused the government of trying to stop people from travelling to Delhi to take part in the protest.
Rahul Gandhi has appealed to people to turn up in large numbers. "Don't worry about the police, don't worry about lathis [batons] - the BJP will not have the guts to try any of their antics," he wrote on X.
His comments come amid growing concerns about the policing of recent protests in the capital.
On 10 October, thousands of security personnel were deployed and large parts of the city were shut down to thwart protests called by the CJP against CEC Gyanesh Kumar.
All of the top CJP leaders were detained and many demonstrators were beaten and dragged through the streets to break up their protests. BBC reporters covering demonstrationssaw,externalpolice dragging away protesters and using batons on some of them.
The CJP has publicly backed the INDIA bloc rally, but it is unclear whether its senior leaders will attend.

title: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
summary: The cyber-attack, which the company describes as complex, is believed to be the largest ever of its kind.
body:
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after$6.3bn (£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist.
The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.
Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit.
The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds.
America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.
While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort.
The hack also involved some US-linked assets, such as stablecoins Tether and Circle – cryptocurrencies pegged to the dollar.
Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".
It had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected".
Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person. Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach."
Teng also describes how the hackers used "a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate".
Initially, the company had indicated the breach "may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" but later statements have pointed to a broader breach.
In a later update, the firm said it had "set aside" more than $6.34B in company funds to cover the stolen assets and was "actively buying" a range of crypto tokens.
The Binance hack spooked cryptocurrency markets on Friday. The price of Bitcoin was down 5% to $76,800 in Friday afternoon trading in New York.
Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase was down 12% as investors also reacted to earnings results in which the firm reported revenue slightly below expectations. Robinhood, a financial services company that trades in cryptocurrency, was down 7.8%.
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets under its custody.
A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.
The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm.
But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry.
Several experts have warned customers not to regard Binance's promise to cover losses as legally binding and said they may need to pursue litigation to recover them.
Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it".
Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.
Meanwhile, AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said that several elements of the attack resembled earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
In the last five years the crypto industry has been beset by enormous losses from hackers.
In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor. The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.
North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.
North Korea has always denied this, but the wealth of evidence from cryptocurrency flow analysis and insider interviews from defectors is compelling.
It makes North Korea likely to be the only nation that uses hacking as a way to raise public funds.

title: US tech stocks see sharp falls as AI spending nears $1tn
summary: Shares in Intel continue to fall while the tech-heavy Nasdaq opens at its lowest level in more than two months.
body:
Tech stocks tumbled for the second day in a row as concerns rise over the hundreds of billions of dollars firms are investing in artificial intelligence (AI).
Shares in Intel plummeted by 28% on Friday, while Google owner Alphabet saw its stock price continue to fall another 1.4% after a 12% plunge on Thursday.
Other tech stocks, including Reddit and Amazon also fell, while the Nasdaq index of the largest tech firms listed in the US, ended October with its worst monthly slide since March 2025.
While tech firms are spending big on AI, their earnings are not always meeting analysts' expectations, spooking investors and creating fears of an AI bubble.
Major tech companies have ramped up artificial intelligence spending, with Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft committing to spending $800bn between them in 2026.
Alphabet's stock market value fell sharply on Thursday,taking more than $500bn (£374bn) off its market valueafter it revealed the AI summaries it now provides as the top answer to search queries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.
At the same time, Alphabet expects to spend up to $205bn this year on investments, almost entirely related to AI.
The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere however, with Intel shedding more than $130bn in value.
The chip maker said it planned to increase spending on AI despite weaker demand for computers, a major source of demand for its micro-processors.
On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.
"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.
In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.
Amazon on Thursday revealed it had also spent more cash than it was making, and that spending had increased six-fold over the span of three months.
The company has committed to spending $220bn this year, putting the money towards investments such as AI data centres, network equipment, and servers.
Amazon shares recovered some overnight losses, but were still down by 1.4% at the end of Friday trading.
Reddit stock plunged by 29%, after the social media platform revealed weaker-than-expected daily user figures and warned that Google's growing AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic.
Stock in online game platform Roblox also fell, down by 18%, as its daily active user numbers dropped.
Several major tech firms have reported earnings this week, including Microsoft, and analysts said there were questions about the payout from the huge investments in AI.
Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google.
He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out".
"The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."
Many analysts have been debating the possibility of an AI bubble in the stock market.
The worry is that some tech firms will not be able to justify their sky-high valuations because the cost of building AI data centres and developing the software will end up being greater than the money they can make from it.
Kathleen Brookes, research director at trading firm XTB, said there have been many ups and downs in AI trade in recent months.
"Investors have turned ruthless, punishing any signs of disappointment in [third quarter] earnings," she said.
"The AI trade has had a good run in recent years, but now investors want payback, and companies like Alphabet and Intel are in the crosshairs."
However, stock market values for many of these companies remain well above where they were a year ago.
While the Nasdaq closed 2.8% lower, it is up 7.8% over the last year. Similarly Amazon is up nearly 8% over the past 12 months, while Alphabet is down 1.3%.
Brookes noted that November is typically a strong month for stocks.
"If we see AI stocks continue to struggle in the coming days, it could suggest the AI trade is past its peak, and investors will be looking for a new theme to drive markets," she said.

title: City of London chief tops UK Black Powerlist
summary: Ian Thomas, who heads the City of London Corporation, tops the Black Powerlist in its 21st year.
body:
Ian Thomas, chief executive of the City of London Corporation, has been named the UK's most influential Black Briton in this year's Black Powerlist awards.
The 57-year old is the first Black person to oversee the Square Mile's governing body in its more than 900-year history.
The City of London Corporation is an administrative body with responsibility for London's central financial district, headed by its own Lord Mayor.
Thomas tops the 2027 Black Powerlist, which recognises the most powerful people of African and Caribbean heritage in the UK.
The award body said he was "a respected public-service leader with over 30 years' experience in local government".
Other influential names in this year's top ten include entrepreneurs Emma Grede and Steven Bartlett, as well as actor and filmmaker Sir Idris Elba.
Comedian Sir Lenny Henry has also been recognised, with a Lifetime Achievement award, for co-founding Comic Relief, which has raised over £1.6bn since 1985.
Now in its 21st year, the Black Powerlist celebrates people who have broken through barriers to reach leadership roles, thereby inspiring future generations.
"It exists to show young people of African and Caribbean heritage what is possible, in fields they might never have considered," said Michael Eboda, the list's publisher.
Sir Lenny Henry is being honoured with a Lifetime Achievement Award
Thomas said he secured the role at the head of the City of London Corporation in 2022 only following seven interviews and an election.
'When I started my journey in public service, I never, ever thought, [not] in a million years, that I'd be recognised in this way," he told the BBC.
As chief executive, he oversees around 5,000 staff with responsibilities including the City of London Police, 11,000 acres of open spaces such as Epping Forest and Hampstead Heath, and advocacy for the UK's financial and professional services sector.
Thomas was born in Sheffield to parents who made the city their home after leaving Jamaica as part of the Windrush generation.
"They worked incredibly hard and instilled that sense of discipline and respect, and that's the core of how I do business," he said of his upbringing.
Growing up, Thomas aspired to be a footballer and took part in trials alongside Alan Shearer.
Reflecting on his own change of direction, Thomas joked it was about "following dreams and if they don't come true… there's always something else".
Before joining the City of London Corporation, Thomas served as chief executive of the Royal Borough of Kingston upon Thames where he oversaw public services and a £1.2bn regeneration programme.
He was appointed a CBE in the 2019 New Year Honours in the wake of the Rotherham Abuse scandal for transforming children's services during his time as strategic director for children and young people at Rotherham Metropolitan Borough Council.
Thomas replaces last year's incumbent, Afua Kyei, the Bank of England's chief financial officer and executive director, and is joined on this year's list by Comfort Ero, the President and chief executive of the International Crisis Group, who takes second place.

title: How Poundland grew from a market stall to a high street giant
summary: The retail giant - which started life at a Wolverhampton market - is now at threat of collapse.
body:
Poundland has been a recognisable presence on high streets for more than 35 years
"When I told people what I wanted to do, open shops on the high street selling things for one pound, they said, 'how will you find products to sell for a pound, what about inflation, it will never work.'"
That is how Steve Smith, the founder of Poundland, describes the genesis of the budget giant - which went on to employ thousands of people and see over a million customers a week -on his own website,external.
But now the West Midlands-based retailer is teetering on the edge, after its US-based owners Gordon Brothers cut off a vital funding supply and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group.
Poundland staff protest after chain approach administrators
Burnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapse
The curious case of why Poundland is struggling during a cost-of-living crisis
Having spent time on his parents stall since the age of two Wolverhampton-born businessman Smith started out in the very same place - selling items for £1 from his own stall.
After a £50,000 loan from his parents he opened the first Poundland shop, in The Octagon Shopping Centre in Burton-upon-Trent, Staffordshire, on 13 December 1990.
That first day, with a range of 624 products, the store took more than £13,000 - "and Poundland was born," Smith said.
Smith and his wife, Tracy, now based in Shropshire, owned the company for 16 years.
In 2006, he decided the time had come and he sold his final shares in the business for £250m, but later said the sale felt it was "as though somebody had died".
Steven Smith founded Poundland in 1990 with the help of his father, Kevin Smith
But by 2025,the Walsall-based company was itself sold for just £1.
Its owner, Polish firm Pepco, confirmed it had sold the brand for a "nominal" sum to US investment firm Gordon Brothers.
At the time Poundland had more than 800 stores across the UK and Ireland and employed around 16,000 staff.
"I did pick up the phone when I heard it was for sale but I was a bit too late," Smith said after the sale.
Now, the retailer's bosses have filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which will give the business 10 days to find a rescue deal.
A protest was held outside the Poundland HQ on Thursday, Claire Sutcliffe - who has been at the company for nearly a decade - among those demonstrating.
Sutcliffe said she was "very sad" to hear the news
Questioned about how she felt, the 49-year-old replied she was "very sad", adding: "Nine years is a lot working for Poundland and they've been really good to me as a Poundland family, really supportive."
Sutcliffe added that some had worked for the business for 20 years and "it's just very sad for us all".
Asked what her message was to owners Gordon Brothers, she replied: "Please just sell.
"Save our jobs, we've all got families to feed and it's... near Christmas."
About 25 people took part in a protest at Poundland in Walsall on Thursday
Professor Sarah Montano, a retail expert from the University of Birmingham, said: "The real problem for Poundland is, when they first started it was really great because everything was £1, that was a really unique selling point for them.
"[Today] there's competitors which are offering very similar prices and for quite a lot of products they're offering them cheaper."
She added that some competitors had "really got their finger on the key trends".
In a statement, the board of Poundland Limited said it had been "working on a formal sale process for Poundland" and despite "enormous efforts it has not been possible to identify an acceptable offer for the business as a whole".
"The process has however attracted several established retail operators who have made formal offers, collectively these cover a significant part of the business, and we believe offer the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and to preserve jobs," they said.
"We recognise any sale process creates uncertainty and particularly when set against a challenging UK economic environment."
They also thanked "staff, suppliers and customers for their continued support".

title: Burnham 'open' to calls for slavery apology but not reparations
summary: The British government has never formally apologised for slavery despite repeated calls from a number of Commonwealth leaders.
body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he is "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but has ruled out financial reparations.
He said he wanted a "dialogue with those affected" and was open to "calls for an apology", but said reparations were "not the right answer".
The statement was welcomed by the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) for Afrikan Reparations, with its chairwoman Bell Ribeiro-Adday telling BBC Radio 4's Today programme the issue was not just about money.
It comes ahead of next week's Commonwealth leaders summit in the Caribbean. AsKing Charles III tours the region, there have been renewed calls for an apology.
During the first leg of his tour in the Bahamas, the King made reference to the "suffering of the past". Later, in Guyana, he visited the site of a rebellion of enslaved people against British authorities.
On Saturday, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade, when Africans were trafficked to the Americas, as a "brutal and barbaric violation" and said Britain must "face up to the past".
The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations. Burnham has stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and has stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.
"I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part," Burnham wrote in apiece for the Guardian,external.
He said Commonwealth countries had for years been asking for an "honest conversation".
He said he wanted to offer a "structured dialogue", adding: "Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process. I am open to them."
Chancellor John Healey told the BBC that Burnham was "open to a discussion" about an apology because it was "the right thing, particularly ahead of the Commonwealth heads conference".
The Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting starts on 1 November in Antigua, and will be opened by the King as part of his tour.
Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg, Healey said the prime minister does not think reparations are the right approach.
He added that a formal apology doesn't mean British people should now "accept the financial liability for any part in things that happened hundreds of years ago in which they had no role".
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was "no reason British taxpayers today should be held financially responsible for things that happened generations before any of us were born."
In a post on X, Badenoch wrote that Labour was "already spending too much on Britain's welfare state, now is not the time for Andy Burnham to be providing global welfare."
Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey said: "I do think we have a duty there and saying sorry is always quite a good thing."
Bell Ribeiro-Addy said that while her parliamentary group welcomed the government's acceptance of the role it played, it had "still fallen short of a formal state apology and that actually costs nothing".
"Acknowledgement is not the same as understanding," she told Today, adding: "Until we apologise, we are never going to be on equal footing… it's meant to be a family of nations - a Commonwealth - and it's simply not the case."
Ribeiro-Addy, who is MP for Clapham and Brixton Hill, said that, to her knowledge, an invoice for financial reparations has not been given to the UK, and so discussing "reparative justice" on those ends, was missing the point.
"My worry is the focus on financial reparations, and I think that is deeply problematic and has not quite listened to what people have said," Ribeiro-Addy said.
Downing Street believes it is in the UK's interest to strengthen the Commonwealth, in a world where China and Russia are seeking to exert influence.
Only this week, President Vladimir Putin hosted a Russia-Africa summit in Moscow.
Steve Rosenberg: Inside the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow
Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley, who has sought reparations, welcomed Burnham's statement, saying she would engage in good faith while still seeking reparatory justice.
Denis O'Brien, founder of The Repair Campaign, said Burnham's statement was disappointing and did not go far enough.
"The British government must stop obfuscating and give a full and formal apology now," he said.
"This would be a significant and symbolic first step towards reparatory justice."
From the 16th Century, English authorities and the monarchy were prominent participants in the centuries-long slave trade.
Burnham is not first UK prime minister to address the issue.
In 2007, the then PM Tony Blairsaid the UK's role in the slave trade was a matter of "deep sorrow and regret".
David Cameron ruled out making reparations for Britain's role in the historic slave trade in 2015,urging Caribbean countries to "move on" during a visit to Jamaica.
Rishi Sunakdismissed a call for the government to apologise and pay reparations for the UK's historical role in slaveryin 2023 after Bell Ribeiro-Addy asked if he would make a "full and meaningful apology" and "commit to reparatory justice".
Sunak replied with a "no", and said: "Trying to unpick our history is not the right way forward."
In 2024, Sir Keir Starmerruled out compensation for the UK's historical role in the slave trade.
At the time, he said he wanted to focus on the future of the Commonwealth.
Britain had a key role in ending the trade, through Parliament's passage of a law to abolish slavery in 1833.
As part of that law, British plantation owners were paid for the loss of people they had enslaved.
The UK only finished paying off the debt it incurred to cover the payments in 2015.

title: Mahmood expected to announce changes to rules around indefinite leave to remain
summary: The home secretary has faced opposition from within the government over plans to impose new rules on migrant workers already in the UK.
body:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is expected to announce her final decision on immigration rules for legal migrants next week.
She had proposed to extend the wait for permanent settlement from the current five years to 10 with some lower-paid migrants facing a 15-year wait. The BBC understands the proposals are likely to be revised for most of those currently  working in social care.
The home secretary was concerned about the number of people who would be eligible for permanent residency after a period of very high net migration under the previous government.
Mahmood has faced opposition from within the government for proposing to impose new rules on migrant workers already in the UK.
Before she rejoined the cabinet, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner described the proposals as "un-British" because they sought to change the rules for people who had come to the UK in good faith.
In particular, many lower-paid social care workers were facing a wait of up to 15 years rather than five.
But the BBC understands that social care workers already in the UK are now likely to be exempt from the longer wait.
But as originally proposed, it is likely most other workers will have to live and work in the UK for 10 years before being eligible for permanent settlement. That can be reduced if they contribute to their local communities or have higher incomes.
The government's consultation on the proposed reforms has drawn 200,000 responses.
The Home Office will not comment on Mahmood's final decisions until they are presented to Parliament in the coming week.
In September, a Conservative spokesperson said: "Shabana Mahmood has caved in to pressure from Angela Rayner and her open borders MPs and will shred her own plans to reform indefinite leave to remain."
"This is a slap in the face to British taxpayers who will have to subsidise low-skilled, low wage migrants."
Permanent residence, or indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.

title: Why MPs keep talking about an early election despite Burnham's denials
summary: The prime minister has categorically ruled out an early general election, but it has not stopped speculation at Westminster.
body:
Wander through Parliament at the moment, and there is one issue many MPs want to discuss: is there going to be an early general election?
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has nearly three years to go before he has to call an election and he has repeatedly and categorically ruled out going to the country early.
But the discussion persists - and many think it is a real possibility.
After Wednesday's Budget, that talk has only increased.
As one former Labour minister puts it: "Why would you sprinkle round a few politically smart (albeit small) giveaways now but delay all the really tough and unpopular decisions on welfare anddefenceto an autumn spending review if you weren't creating a window for a spring election?"
Others have also suggested to the BBC that Chancellor John Healey's plans felt like a pre-election programme.
They argue the Budget contained voter-friendly measures on the cost of living, such as£100 help for many with energy billsand extending VAT cuts on electricity bills. Young voters are to be offered help on to the housing ladder, through theYour First Home scheme.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has questioned why some-voter friendly measures announced by Healey will only be in place until the summer.
Could it be, she suggests, that the prime minister plans to go to the country before these measures run out?
(The counter-argument to this is that household energy pressures are less severe in the summer.)
Some MPs also point out the prime minister is popular at the moment and Labour is leading in most polls.
Reform, who had led the polls for some time, have had a difficult few months.
Will things ever look better for Burnham, they ask.
Andy Burnham arrives to vote in July's Greater Manchester mayoral elections
Then there are the difficult spending decisions faced by the chancellor.
How to find the money to fund an increase in defence spending? How to bring down the welfare bill? How to cut departmental spending to make the books add up?
"He is delaying all of the bad stuff until after a poll," reckons one Conservative MP.
The Liberal Democrats have claimed there is a 30% chance of a general election on 10 December. The party has been put on a "snap election footing".
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has said he thinks there could be a general election in May.
It is worth pointing out predictions of an early election are coming more from opposition MPs, some of whom might be keen to cause a bit of trouble.
An election has to be held by August 2029, but some Labour MPs have said they are so convinced an early election is on the way that they have told their staff to prepare for one in the first half of next year.
Burnham was a member of Gordon Brown's losing team in 2010
Healey unveils £100 for energy bills and bank tax in first Budget
Burnham rules out early general election in next 12 months
Analysis: Healey provides some breathing space but things still set to get worse for most
There are, though, plenty of arguments against a general election in the next year.
Firstly, the prime minister has repeatedly ruled it out in interviews.
On Wednesday, he saidexplicitly that there would not be an election in the next 12 months. Politicians can change their minds, but one veteran Tory concludes a change of heart, after emphatic denials, would be too damaging to "Brand Burnham".
Next – despite the chancellor's giveaways on the cost of living – theoverall economic outlookis "pretty grim", in the words of the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).
Real Household Disposable Income looks set to fall in the coming months. Interest rates are predicted to go up. Nobody knows for sure what will happen next in the Middle East – and whether things could get worse before they get better.
Burnham has pledged a rewiring of the British state. He plans to set out a 10-year plan in the coming weeks. But without more detail, some wonder if voters will know enough to make a judgement.
On more than one occasion, Burnham has vowed to bring about the most significant change in British politics in four decades.
One former Labour minister could not detect much in this week's Budget to that effect, saying: "It's not an end to 40 years of neoliberalism is it?"
That message was echoed by another Labour MP: "It was too low key to be an election Budget."
"It was a disappointment, a play it safe, keep everything ticking over Budget… crumbs for all," said another.
"No early general election after that Budget. We would be toast."
Theresa May, pictured here with husband Philip, decided to call a snap election while on a walking holiday
Some argue Burnham would benefit from having his own mandate, with his own manifesto. But given the size of Labour's general election win last time, many MPs think it's inevitable that Labour will lose ground.
Others say that if Burnham's government does feel the need to break Sir Keir Starmer's manifesto commitments by increasing taxes, they should just do it, instead of holding an election.
"If we need an election to put up taxes then arguably that's easier to do now with our massive majority than to start an election campaign on the basis that we're calling it in order to put up taxes," said one Labour MP.
"People act like a manifesto is a legal document written in blood. Plenty of governments have broken lots of manifesto promises."
Remember too that the prime minister has promised a detailed plan on social care in England, which is some way off. He has also not decided how far he wants to go in taking the UK closer to the EU.
There is a lot for Number 10 to weigh up.
Labour might look back to Gordon Brown, whodid not call an early electionwhen he was prime minister and doing well in the polls. If he had gone to the country in October 2007, might Labour have stayed in power?
But there will be plenty of others who look to Theresa May. Sheopted for a snap general electionin April 2017, after mulling the decision over on a walking holiday in Wales. Despite flying high in the polls, the Tories lost their majority.
So will Burnham do it?
He might be tempted. But there are plenty of risks that mean it would be far from an easy choice.

title: 'No nation left behind' says Burnham after meeting first ministers in Glasgow
summary: The meeting involved representatives from the UK's four nations to discuss devolving more powers to regions and cities.
body:
Andy Burnham met the first ministers from Scotland and Wales and representatives from Northern Ireland in Glasgow
The prime minister has said the UK's four nations must "move together" to devolve more power to regions and cities, following a meeting with the Scottish and Welsh first ministers in Glasgow.
Andy Burnham said he wanted to ensure no nation was "left behind" after the sit-down, which also included representatives from Northern Ireland.
SNP leader John Swinney said he welcomed recognition that "Westminster is not working for Scotland" and pledged to work "constructively and collaboratively" with Burnham, while Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iowerth said the meeting was "positive".
Both first ministers have called for a wider conversation about independence but Burnham has ruled out referendums.
Scotland 'not like Manchester', Swinney says in dig at PM Burnham
Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution'
First minister says Budget not serious about Wales ahead of meeting with PM
Speaking after the first National Economic Council for the nations in Glasgow, Burnham highlighted plans for devolution at the regional level, saying he wanted to ensure no nation was "left behind".
"It's really important we all move at the same pace together, and I won't allow anything to delay that," the prime minister said.
"Growth can't wait. People need to see improvements in employment and in living standards in all parts of the UK."
Northern Ireland was represented by officials at the meeting amid thepolitical fallout from the Drumcree parade dispute.
Burnham held talks with first ministers John Swinney (left) and Rhun ap Iowerth (right)
Ministers and representatives at the summit discussed handing regions more powers to control employment support and funding for reindustrialisation.
"It's about creating those structures at a regional level and that is matter for Scotland and Wales to decide what that looks like in both countries," Burnham said.
He urged the Scottish and Welsh governments to "work jointly" with the UK government on "a model of deeper devolution".
In the context of reindustrialisation, Burnham added this could be more devolution of innovation funding.
Swinney, ap Iorwerth and Burnham also agreed during the meeting there are too many young people out of work in the nations.
The prime minister said the UK government would look at "arrangements for further devolution of employment support for young people in both Scotland and Wales".
Devolution has been at the heart of Burnham's policy agenda since he took his place in Downing Street this summer.
He claims "rewiring the state" and handing more control to regional mayors and authorities across England will boost economic growth.
The prime minister's devolution at the national level has so far been less clear but Burnham has said he will listen to the administrations' calls for further powers while advocating that they share more responsibilities with local authorities.
John Swinney said while he and Burnham disagree on independence, the meeting was "a welcome start" on further devolution.
"When the people of Scotland take issues into their own hands, the best outcomes will about," Scotland's first minister said.
"To that end, I will work constructively and collaboratively with the prime minister to devolve more powers from Westminster to Scotland - as long as those proposals drive economic growth that is felt in higher wages, better jobs, more opportunities for business to start and expand, and support with the cost of living."
A Downing Street spokesperson said the UK government would review issues raised by the first minister but this would not include a second independence referendum in Scotland.
Rhun ap Iowerth said: "I was pleased to meet with the prime minister in Glasgow today where I once again pressed the need for Wales and the Welsh government to have the necessary tools to better serve our communities.
"I also reiterated the point that further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd."
He added he welcomed the prime minister's "step forward" on the Welsh government's fiscal and borrowing powers and gave his "full support" in pushing for a stronger relationship with the EU.
The prime minister had "positive discussions" with the Welsh leader, Downing Street said.
A spokesperson added: "The first minister of Wales agreed to start a process to explore how each government could contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode."

title: Streeting denies 'kicking can down the road' in defence spending row
summary: The government is under pressure to set out a path to greater defence spending, as ministers unveil plans to boost UK firms.
body:
Wes Streeting has defended the government's current approach
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has denied "kicking the can down the road" over how much the UK spends on defence.
The government has faced criticism for not setting out a pathway at Wednesday's Budget to hit its target of spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.
Streeting is at odds with MPs on the Commons defence committee over the issue.
It comes as Chancellor John Healey and Streeting announce that foreign firms which are awarded defence contracts of more than £50m will need to invest an equal value back into the UK.
Under the new investment rules, described as an "offset strategy", these companies will need to spend an equivalent amount on British factories, jobs and training.
The Ministry of Defence will apply the rules on a "case-by-case" basis from April 2027, the government said. Healey and Streeting will unveil the policy on a visit to UK defence contractor BAE's shipbuilding site in Glasgow later.
Countries including Poland, Norway and the Netherlands have mandated similar rules to "boost the economic benefit from defence procurement", the government said.
While ministers hope the rules increase investment in Britain's defence industry, they appear designed to do so in a politically palatable way rather than committing to spending cuts.
Tan Dhesi, Labour chair of the cross-party Commons defence committee, said on Wednesday that decisions had been "kicked into the long grass" to next year's government spending review, rather thanannounced in the Budget.
He warned that without building capabilities now, "we risk leaving ourselves seriously vulnerable in the event of a major conflict".
Streeting hit back at these comments as "unfair" and "unfounded".
Speaking on Thursday, Dhesi said the committee stands by its criticism.
"We had hoped to see that the chancellor would set out a precise pathway to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030," Dhesi told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
"But instead some of those key decisions on defence have lamentably been delayed until next year's spending review."
He praised the government for plugging a £4.7bn hole in the Defence Investment Plan in the Budget, through asking government departments tocut their capital budgets by 1%.
Labour MP Tan Dhesi has led the latest criticism of government defence spending
Responding on Thursday, Streeting told Today: "I like Tan very much, he's a friend and I respect him, but I strongly disagree with him.
"And I don't think the charge he makes of delaying or kicking the can down the road stacks up against the extra money that is already going into defence and the capability we're funding right now."
Streeting told BBC Breakfast the new rules, aiming to create "bang for the British buck", would help achieve this target given increasing defence spending "does come at a cost to the country and other things we'd like to spend money on".
He said waiting for the spending review, which does not have a fixed date and could come in the second half of 2027, was "the right thing to do" so ministers can look at "spending in the round".
He added that the UK was ready to deal with hostile threats, but "we're not where we'd want to be".
"There's no sugarcoating the fact that our Armed Forces were under-invested in for more than a decade," he told Breakfast.
Defence analysts have questioned the government's ability to deliver on its 2030 target and theNato-wide target of 3.5%by 2035. UK defence spending is at an estimated 2.6% of GDP this year.
Some estimates have suggested the government will need to spend an additional £10bn annually to reach its targets.
Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said on Wednesday that Healey "failed his own test" by not setting out a "plan for 3%".
Healey resigned as then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June over not spending enough on defence.
In the Budget, Healey said the UK was negotiating with Finland, Poland and the Netherlands to set up an international bank - the Multilateral Defence Mechanism - to boost defence investment and joint procurement.
But Conservative shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge said this amounted to "turning to borrowing at a time when the national debt is over £3 trillion".
"The answer is not more borrowing – it's to cut welfare to fund defence," he said.
